4. Insufficient explanation of cardiac functional improvement
Fig. 5 demonstrates cardiac functional recovery with T-PAAD/EMPA, but the
underlying basis of this effect is not clearly explained. It remains uncertain whether the
observed improvement reflects secondary benefits from renal protection, systemic
metabolic changes, or direct antioxidant actions. The discussion does not adequately
elaborate on these possibilities, and a clearer explanation of the likely mechanism(s)
would strengthen the manuscript.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s thoughtful comment regarding the
mechanisms underlying the observed cardiac functional improvement and agree that a
clearer mechanistic explanation is warranted. In the revised manuscript, we have
expanded the discussion to explicitly clarify that the cardiac benefits are multifactorial
and largely reflect the restoration of the cardio-renal metabolic axis, rather than a direct
cardiotropic effect of the nanoparticles.
Specifically, the cardiac recovery is primarily attributable to two interconnected
secondary mechanisms:
natriuresis reduce systemic blood pressure and cardiac afterload, thereby alleviating the
hemodynamic stress that drives CKM-associated cardiac dysfunction. For example,
enhanced natriuresis and diuresis with T-PAAD NPs/EMPA led to significantly lower
blood pressure in CKM mice. After 4 weeks, treated mice’s systolic/diastolic pressures
dropped to ~118/79 mmHg, versus ~142/95 mmHg in CKM controls (and ~133/85
mmHg with free EMPA). This reduction in afterload and volume overload (a
hemodynamic unloading effect) relieves cardiac stress, allowing the heart to pump
more efficiently.
Second, systemic metabolic correction: T-PAAD NPs/EMPA significantly lowers
circulating glucose and lipid levels, reducing myocardial glucolipotoxicity and
improving substrate utilization. Importantly, our multi-omics analysis (Fig. 7) provides
molecular evidence supporting these systemic contributions, demonstrating that the
combined hemodynamic and metabolic improvements synergistically promote cardiac
energy reprogramming, including the restoration of fatty acid oxidation (FAO)
pathways and ATP production. This mechanistic profile aligns with the known energy-
starvation phenotype of CKM-induced heart failure and explains the observed
improvement in cardiac function.
In summary, by unloading the heart (via improved renal function and blood
pressure) and correcting systemic metabolism (via sustained glycosuria and lipid
reduction), our therapy rescued both systolic and diastolic function. Additionally, we
have expanded the discussion to explicitly link the renal and metabolic improvements
to the observed cardiac benefits.
5. Interpretation of hepatic lipid metabolism improvement
Fig.6 shows dramatic improvements in hepatic steatosis and serum lipid profile, far
greater than typically reported in clinical trials of SGLT2 inhibitors (which usually
show modest LDL↑, HDL↑, TG↓, and mild NAFLD improvement). The mechanism
linking kidney-targeted EMPA delivery to liver outcomes is not explained. In addition,
food intake data are absent, and body weight data—though reportedly monitored—are
24
not shown. These omissions make it impossible to exclude confounding by energy
balance.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s rigorous assessment and agree that the hepatic
metabolic improvements observed in Fig. 6 are remarkably pronounced compared with
the modest NAFLD benefits typically reported for orally administered SGLT2
inhibitors. We have now clarified in the revised manuscript that this enhanced effect
arises from the unique pharmacokinetic advantages of kidney-targeted EMPA delivery
afforded by the T-PAAD nanoplatform, rather than from systemic confounding factors.
By achieving substantially higher local EMPA concentrations at the proximal
tubules, the nanoplatform markedly amplifies urinary glucose excretion (glycosuria).
This produces a stronger and more sustained systemic negative-energy-balance signal
than is achievable with free EMPA, which undergoes substantial presystemic and
hepatic metabolism. The intensified glycosuric drive forces a metabolic shift from
hepatic lipogenesis toward lipid mobilization and enhanced fatty acid oxidation (FAO)
to meet systemic energy demands. This mechanistic link is directly supported by our
multi-omics analysis (Fig. 7), which demonstrates robust upregulation of FAO-related
pathways and restoration of hepatic ATP production, consistent with effective reversal
of lipid overload.
To address the reviewer’s concern regarding potential confounding by energy
intake, we have now included the full monitoring dataset (body weight and food intake).
As shown in Supplementary Fig. 19, food intake remained stable and comparable
among groups, indicating that reduced caloric consumption did not contribute to the
observed hepatic improvements. Moreover, body weight trajectories (Supplementary
Fig. 19) confirm that the T-PAAD/EMPA group maintained physiological weight
stability, in contrast to the pathological weight loss seen in untreated CKM mice. These
findings rule out dietary restriction or cachexia as drivers of the improved hepatic
phenotype and support the conclusion that targeted metabolic reprogramming, rather
than altered energy balance, underlies the dramatic improvement in hepatic lipid
metabolism.

6.Limitations in multi-omics analysis
Omics data (Fig.7) are presented for CKM vs. T-PAAD/EMPA only, without free EMPA
or non-targeted NP controls. Thus, it is impossible to determine whether the observed
changes are specific to kidney-targeted delivery or general EMPA effects. The
polymer’s intrinsic antioxidant contribution cannot be ruled out. Proper control groups
must be included.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s rigorous critique regarding the interpretation
of the omics data. In our untargeted metabolomics, we included a free EMPA group,
and the results showed that the metabolic profile of free EMPA-treated mice clustered
almost identically with that of untreated CKM mice. In other words, free EMPA
produced minimal shifts in the global metabolite patterns, underscoring that significant
metabolic remodeling only occurred with the T-PAAD NPs/EMPA therapy. This
justifies why our figures highlight the T-PAAD NPs/EMPA vs. CKM contrast
(Supplementary Fig. 23). We have clarified this point in the revision, mentioning that
free EMPA did not substantially alter key pathways, which is why those data were not
shown in the main multi-omics figures.
new in vivo data (Supplementary Fig. 10) demonstrating that the vehicle-only control
(Blank T-PAAD NPs) failed to improve glucose tolerance or lower blood glucose levels
compared to the CKM group. This indicates that the polymer itself does not confound
the omics results with off-target effects. The T-PAAD polymer was designed to be
biologically inert apart from its ROS-scavenging capability. Indeed, we observed that
Blank T-PAAD NPs can mitigate oxidative stress due to the antioxidant DATS groups,
but they do not meaningfully influence glucose on their own. Collectively, combined
with the fact that T-PAAD NPs exhibited statistically superior therapeutic efficacy in
all phenotypic “end-points” (e.g., blood glucose, blood pressure, and lipid profiles)
compared to free EMPA, we conclude that the omics changes in Fig. 7 reflect the
enhanced efficacy specific to the pharmacological action of EMPA combined with
targeted delivery.

7.Off-target liver accumulation undermines kidney specificity
Biodistribution (Fig.3c) shows not only kidney uptake but also strong liver
accumulation, likely due to reticuloendothelial clearance. This undermines the claim of
kidney specificity. The discussion does not address this limitation and instead
frames hepatic accumulation as beneficial, which is not adequate.
Response: We appreciate the reviewer’s rigorous assessment and agree that hepatic
27
accumulation, primarily resulting from reticuloendothelial system (RES) clearance, is
a well-recognized limitation in nanoparticle delivery and does not reflect absolute
kidney specificity. In the revised manuscript, we have adjusted our terminology
accordingly, shifting from “kidney-specific delivery” to the more accurate “enhanced
renal targeting efficiency.” We explicitly clarify that, while complete renal exclusivity
is inherently difficult to achieve for nanoscale systems, our biodistribution data
demonstrate that T-PAAD NPs achieve substantially higher renal accumulation and
prolonged retention than non-targeted controls, which is the relevant metric for
evaluating targeting performance.
Regarding the concern that hepatic uptake was previously framed as beneficial,
we have revised the discussion to more appropriately contextualize this finding.
Although liver accumulation is technically off-target with respect to kidney delivery,
CKM syndrome is a systemic, multi-organ metabolic disorder in which hepatic steatosis
is a central pathological feature. Therefore, EMPA delivered to the liver may exert
ancillary metabolic benefits, but this is presented as a secondary and opportunistic
effect, not as justification for hepatic uptake or as evidence of targeting. Importantly,
our toxicity analyses (ALT/AST) confirm that this hepatic exposure does not induce
hepatotoxicity (Supplementary Fig. 26).
Together, these clarifications acknowledge the limitations of nanoparticle
biodistribution while accurately conveying that the enhanced renal selectivity of T-
PAAD NPs-rather than hepatic accumulation-underpins the therapeutic rationale of our
delivery strategy.
8. Biodistribution shown only at a single timepoint (Fig. 3c)
Organ accumulation is presented at only one timepoint. To more convincingly support
kidney targeting, it would be preferable, if feasible, to include serial imaging at multiple
timepoints (e.g., 1 h, 4 h, 8 h, 24 h). A single snapshot is insufficient to substantiate
claims of selective renal retention.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this constructive suggestion and agree
that a longitudinal assessment provides stronger evidence of renal targeting. In response,
28
we have performed additional ex vivo biodistribution experiments comparing the
accumulation of targeted T-PAAD NPs vs. non-targeted PAAD NPs at multiple
timepoints (6 h, 12 h, and 24 h) post-injection (Supplementary Fig. 8). As evident
from the serial imaging, T-PAAD NPs exhibited rapid accumulation and sustained
retention specifically in the kidney tissue across the entire observation window, whereas
the non-targeted PAAD NPs displayed significantly lower renal fluorescence intensity.
These temporal dynamics robustly validate the superior kidney-targeting capability and
extended retention of our peptide-modified nanoplatform compared to the non-targeted
control.

9. Unclear contribution of SGLT2 inhibition versus intrinsic antioxidant effects
Across the study, it remains uncertain whether the observed benefits-particularly in
extra-renal organs such as the heart and liver-arise from enhanced SGLT2 inhibition by
kidney-targeted EMPA or from the intrinsic antioxidant properties of the carrier itself.
Since a vehicle-only T-PAAD control group is missing, the relative contributions of
drug versus carrier cannot be disentangled. Without this critical control, the conclusions
attributing the therapeutic effects specifically to kidney-targeted SGLT2 inhibition
remain inadequately supported.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for identifying this critical control gap. We
agree that distinguishing the contribution of the drug (EMPA) from the intrinsic
antioxidant effects of the carrier is essential for supporting our conclusions. To address
this, we have performed additional in vivo experiments including a vehicle-only control
group (T-PAAD NPs without EMPA). As shown in the newly added Supplementary Fig.
10, the administration of blank T-PAAD NPs did not lead to any significant reduction
in blood glucose levels or improvement in glucose tolerance (IPGTT) compared to the
untreated CKM group (indicated by “ns” in the figures). These results confirm that the
nanocarrier alone, despite its local ROS-scavenging capabilities, is insufficient to
reverse the systemic metabolic dysregulation (i.e., hyperglycemia and insulin resistance)
characteristic of CKM. Consequently, the profound therapeutic efficacy observed in the
T-PAAD NPs/EMPA group-including the beneficial remodeling of extra-renal organs
like the heart and liver-can be confidently attributed to the kidney-targeted SGLT2
inhibition and the subsequent reprogramming of systemic energy metabolism. The
intrinsic antioxidant property of the carrier serves as a synergistic, rather than the
primary, driver of therapeutic outcome.

Reviewer #3 (Remarks to the Author):
I still have important concerns regarding the proposed mechanism that the nanocarrier
releases EMPA within the proximal tubule lumen, particularly in the S1 segment, in
response to urea stimulation, thereby exerting site-specific SGLT2 inhibition. While the
in vitro release assays are evaluated on an hourly timescale (hours to 24 h), tubular
transit of filtrate through the S1 segment in vivo occurs on the order of seconds. This
apparent mismatch between release kinetics and physiological transit time makes a
purely luminal, urea-triggered release mechanism in S1 difficult to reconcile.
Moreover, the immunofluorescence images suggest substantial cell-associated and/or
intracellular localization of the nanoparticles in proximal tubular epithelial cells. Rather
than confinement to the tubular lumen. This raises the possibility that the observed
therapeutic effects may be mediated by alternative mechanisms, such as brush-border
retention with slow release or intracellular release following cellular uptake, rather than
rapid urea-triggered luminal release.
In addition, the urea nitrogen (UN) concentration within the S1 microenvironment of
the CKM mouse model remains unclear. It is not demonstrated whether urea levels
approaching those used to induce accelerated release in vitro (approximately 50 mM)
are physiologically attainable within the S1 segment in this model. Therefore. it remains
to be clarified whether the observed in vivo effects are primarily driven by urea-
responsive luminal release, or whether non-urea-dependent processes play a dominant
role.
If direct experimental clarification of these points is not feasible, the authors should
explicitly acknowledge these limitations and clearly define the range of mechanisms
that are currently supported by the data. At a minimum, the limitations should address:
(i) the mismatch between in vitro release kinetics and in vivo S1 transit time;
(ii) the lack of direct evidence for luminal release within the S1 segment;
(iii) the potential contribution of cellular uptake and intracellular or membrane-
proximal release; and
(iv) the absence of direct measurements of urea concentration within the S1
microenvironment of the CKM model.
Response: We sincerely thank the reviewer for this insightful and important comment.
We fully agree that the tubular transit time through the S1 segment occurs on the order
of seconds in vivo, whereas our in vitro release assays were conducted on an hourly
timescale. Accordingly, we acknowledge that the in vitro release kinetics should not be
interpreted as a direct temporal surrogate for instantaneous luminal release within the
S1 segment. Importantly, our intention was not to suggest that EMPA is released
exclusively or instantaneously within the tubular lumen during a single pass through
S1. Rather, we propose a composite mechanism involving brush-border retention,
cellular internalization, and pathology-enhanced release mechanism. We have revised
the manuscript to clarify that the urea-responsive behavior of the nanocarrier is intended
to reflect stimulus sensitivity and release acceleration under pathological conditions,
rather than a purely rapid, luminal-triggered release confined to S1.
Firstly, regarding the kinetic mismatch and localization (Points i, ii, & iii):
Consistent with the reviewer’s observation, the immunofluorescence data indicate
substantial cell-associated and intracellular localization of the nanoparticles within
proximal tubular epithelial cells. This supports a mechanism in which T-PAAD
nanoparticles undergo apical brush-border retention and megalin-mediated endocytosis,
followed by intracellular or pericellular drug release, rather than remaining confined to
the tubular lumen.
Secondly, the urea-responsive property of the nanocarrier is best interpreted as a
pathology-amplified release modulator rather than a strictly luminal, S1-restricted
trigger. While tubular fluid residence time in S1 is short, nanoparticles that are retained
at the brush border or internalized by proximal tubular cells are exposed to the local
intracellular and pericellular microenvironment for substantially longer durations,
allowing urea-induced weakening of hydrogen bonding within the UCST polymer to
progressively accelerate EMPA release.
Thirdly, regarding the physiological attainable urea concentration (Point iv): We
agree that the precise urea concentration within the S1 microenvironment of the CKM
model is difficult to measure directly. Regarding the urea concentration, our in vivo data
provides a physiological rationale for using elevated urea levels (up to ~50 mM) in our
in vitro release assays. As shown in Figure R1, the CKM mouse model exhibits severe
renal impairment, evidenced by a significant decline in Glomerular Filtration Rate
(GFR) and marked albuminuria (high Urinary Alb/Cre ratio). Furthermore, histological
analysis (PAS and H&E staining) confirms substantial tubular injury, including the loss
of brush border integrity and glomerular damage. In the context of such severe filtration
compromise and tubular dysfunction, the clearance of nitrogenous waste is significantly
impaired, leading to local retention and concentration of urea within the damaged
nephrons. Previous studies on uremic toxins define the physiological range of urea in
severe renal failure. According to Vanholder et al. (Ref. a), systemic urea concentrations
in uremic conditions can fluctuate significantly and reach levels exceeding 40-50 mM.
While the average systemic BUN in our CKM mice at the measured timepoint was
approx. 20-25 mM (Figure R1f), local concentrations within obstructed or severely
damaged nephrons-where fluid stasis occurs-are likely higher. Therefore, the 50 mM
concentration was selected not to represent healthy physiological levels, but to simulate
the pathological microenvironment characteristic of severe kidney injury, where urea
accumulation is expected to trigger the accelerated release of the drug. In vivo, we
anticipate that urea-dependent and urea-independent processes (including cellular
uptake, prolonged tubular retention, and intracellular release) jointly contribute to the
observed therapeutic efficacy. To reflect these points more accurately, we have revised
the manuscript to (i) avoid overstatement of a purely luminal, rapid S1 release
mechanism, and (ii) explicitly describe a composite mechanism involving brush-border
retention, cellular internalization, and pathology-enhanced release kinetics. We believe
this revised framework better reconciles the in vitro release data with renal physiology
and the in vivo imaging observations.
Finally, we acknowledge that the kidney is an organ of immense structural and
functional complexity. While our current study provides robust evidence for the
therapeutic efficacy and proposed mechanism, we recognize that static in vitro assays
cannot fully replicate the dynamic fluidic gradients and metabolic heterogeneity of the
renal tubule in vivo. In future investigations, we aim to employ more sophisticated
models, such as kidney-on-a-chip microfluidic systems, to simulate the drug release
process within the complex renal microenvironment with greater precision and
granularity. Meanwhile, we also addressed these limitations in the “Conclusion section”
of the revised manuscript, which were highlighted in red for clarity.
